propositions.text: CELL is designated by MC as a recognized inspector and authorized service provider under an agreement with MC.
Mr. Lamontagne is applicant and president of CELL, a recognized technician by MC, with employees Cathy Lamontagne and Éric Potvin.
CELL and its employees were authorized to inspect and certify measuring devices under the Weights and Measures Act.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 1 states that CELL is designated by MC as inspector and service provider, Mr. Lamontagne is president and technician, and CELL authorized to inspect devices.

propositions.text: MC is a department responsible for ensuring measurement accuracy in sales and approving and inspecting measuring devices.
MC administers the Act and designates FSAs and inspectors and enforces conditions attached to these roles.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 2 explains MC's role as department responsible for measurement accuracy, device approval, and designation of FSAs and inspectors.

propositions.text: On September 18, 2018, MC suspended CELL's certificate for failing to remedy two infractions and submit corrective action plans.
CELL and Mr. Lamontagne vigorously contested the suspension through three internal MC appeals.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 3 states MC suspended CELL's certificate for infractions; CELL and Mr. Lamontagne contested suspension through three appeals.

propositions.text: On September 9, 2022, MC President Ms. Allen rejected CELL's third appeal of the suspension (the Decision).

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 4 states MC President Allen rejected CELL's third appeal of suspension on September 9, 2022.

propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review of the Decision, asking court to quash it and declare CELL an FSA and restore inspection powers.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 5 states applicants seek judicial review to quash Decision and restore CELL's FSA status and inspection powers.

propositions.text: The suspension, appeals, MC decisions, and communications form a complex factual background requiring key event narration.
On Feb 23, 2018, follow-up exam of Ms. Lamontagne showed failure on six standardized test methods (MEN).
Mr. Potvin also had a practical exam same day; suspension stems from Ms. Lamontagne's exam.
On Feb 28, 2018, CELL requested copy of Ms. Lamontagne's evaluation report from inspector.
On Mar 1, 2018, MC informed CELL Ms. Lamontagne must submit exam results to complete surveillance.
On Mar 1, 2018, CELL submitted exam results via MC's online application ADEL.
On Mar 2, 2018, MC informed Mr. Lamontagne exam certificate was non-compliant with ADEL user manual.
Between Mar 5 and Apr 3, 2018, email exchanges occurred to complete follow-up exam and correct certificate in ADEL.
On Apr 10, 2018, CELL's lawyer requested MC to provide follow-up exam results and reports.
On Jun 4, 2018, MC responded explaining follow-up exam aimed to assess inspection work and maintain skills.
MC found Ms. Lamontagne did not maintain skills; two infraction reports resulted.
Infraction 1: CELL failed to ensure technician maintained knowledge; six MEN not completed or done properly.
Infraction 2: CELL failed to accurately determine and record exam results; certificate did not reflect device performance.
On Jun 28, 2018, CELL submitted first version of corrective action plans.
On Jul 5, 2018, MC advised CELL plan was non-compliant as it lacked cause explanation and solutions to prevent recurrence.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 6 narrates key events from Feb to Jul 2018 about follow-up exam failures, infractions, certificate issues, and corrective plan submissions.

propositions.text: The Act aims to reduce measurement errors and increase fairness in Canadian market effectively.
Section 8 requires MC to approve, inspect, and certify measuring devices used in commerce per Act and regulations.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 7 states the Act's purpose to reduce errors and MC's duty to approve and certify measuring devices under section 8.

propositions.text: Section 16.1 authorizes Minister to designate persons as inspectors for Act administration and enforcement.
Minister must ensure designated persons are trained and qualified uniformly and conduct exams consistently.
Minister may suspend or revoke any designation under section 16.1.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 8 explains section 16.1 empowering Minister to designate inspectors, ensure training, and suspend or revoke designations.

propositions.text: MC established a registration program authorizing FSAs to examine and certify devices, with terms and conditions.
Program includes modalities, guide, requirements, follow-up exams, infractions, suspensions, and appeal process.
FSAs must comply with MC policies and procedures and sign registration agreement defining scope of authorized devices.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 9 describes MC's registration program for FSAs with conditions, requirements, infractions, and appeal process.

propositions.text: Recognized technicians employed by FSAs must be evaluated and recognized by MC to examine devices.
Technicians must follow MC standardized procedures and pass periodic follow-up exams to maintain powers.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 10 states recognized technicians must be evaluated, follow procedures, and pass follow-up exams to maintain powers.

propositions.text: During follow-up exam, MC inspector observes technician's compliance with standardized test methods (MEN).
MEN ensure technicians and inspectors perform tests consistently.
Technician or FSA must declare test results in ADEL generating exam certificate, which MC inspector reviews for compliance.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 11 explains follow-up exams observe technician's MEN compliance, results declared in ADEL, and MC reviews certificate.

propositions.text: An infraction is any action or omission breaching registration program requirements, Act, regulations, modalities, or agreement.
Infractions include non-compliance with MC policies, bulletins, procedures, or directives including MEN.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 12 defines infraction as any breach of program, Act, regulations, or MC policies including MEN.

propositions.text: If MC finds an infraction, it notifies FSA who must determine causes and implement corrective actions to MC satisfaction.
FSA must implement corrective actions to remedy infractions as required by modalities.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 13 states MC notifies FSA of infractions, requiring cause determination and corrective actions per modalities.

propositions.text: MC may take coercive measures if FSA or technician fails to meet criteria and infractions remain unresolved.
MC considers severity, impact on fairness, intent, and frequency when suspending FSA registration.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 14 states MC may suspend FSA registration considering severity, impact, intent, and frequency of unresolved infractions.

propositions.text: CELL as registered body must ensure all activities comply with program requirements, MC policies, Act, and regulations.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 15 states CELL must ensure compliance with program, MC policies, Act, and regulations.

propositions.text: Decision follows CELL's third appeal of 2018 suspension after full review and discussions with CELL.
MC answered six questions posed by Mr. Lamontagne in third appeal, though some were unrelated to suspension.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 16 states Decision follows third appeal after full review; MC answered six questions from Mr. Lamontagne.

propositions.text: Appeal analysis report attached to Decision lists evaluated points and explains modalities CELL must follow.
Four annexes attached: third appeal, event chronology, technical points from Aug 23 meeting, MC's answers to six questions.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 17 states appeal report attached to Decision lists points evaluated and includes four annexes with relevant documents.

propositions.text: Suspension of CELL is justified and maintained.
CELL failed to meet conditions to maintain inspector designation by not accurately recording inspection results.
CELL did not remedy infractions per designation requirements; corrective plans did not meet program standards despite MC feedback.
MC must suspend technician or registration if FSA fails to meet Act, regulations, or registration conditions.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 18 states suspension justified; CELL failed to meet conditions and remedy infractions; MC must suspend non-compliant FSAs.

propositions.text: Appeal analysis scope set May 16, 2022, to decide if suspension should be maintained or revised.
Appeal process allows complaints but is not negotiation or mediation.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 19 states appeal analysis scope set to review suspension; appeal process allows complaints but not negotiation.

propositions.text: Report details CELL's registration scope, two infractions, correction attempts, program requirements, agreement, responsibilities, MC surveillance, and suspension circumstances.
Infraction 1: Ms. Lamontagne failed to maintain required knowledge; six MEN not respected during Feb 23, 2018 exam.
Infraction 2: Certificate 10294265 did not reflect device performance; CELL failed to accurately record exam results and non-conformities.
Certificate coding did not match comments or MC findings; amended certificate still inconsistent; CELL refused to change certificate.
MC ended surveillance as CELL did not correct certificate per MC requirements and explanations.
Technician and CELL did not adequately determine and record exam results; certificate did not reflect device performance.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 20 details infractions: technician failed MEN, certificate inaccurate, CELL refused correction, MC ended surveillance, infractions confirmed.

propositions.text: MC concluded CELL could not correct the Infractions as three corrective action plans failed regulatory and program requirements despite extensions.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 21 states the earlier decision-maker MC found CELL failed to correct Infractions despite extensions and submitted inadequate corrective plans.

propositions.text: MC conducted surveillance of CELL since 2006 including training, theoretical evaluations, 46 follow-up exams without technician, 13 with technician.
MC's surveillance activities allowed interaction on technical requirements and followed rigorous quality management processes.
During follow-up exams with technician, MC inspectors observe technician's work without much intervention to verify knowledge and compliance with MEN.
MC inspectors do not discuss test methods or issue certificates; recognized technician issues examination certificate in ADEL.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 22 describes earlier decision-maker MC's surveillance activities of CELL, their procedures, and roles during follow-up exams with technicians.

propositions.text: MC collaborated with CELL to resolve issues; observed CELL misunderstood some MEN and regulatory requirements.
MC explained requirements further but Mr. Lamontagne requested MEN changes.
MC sent warning letter granting additional time to correct Infractions; last attempts received August 2 and 7, 2018.
MC found progress on first Infraction but with gaps; CELL requested removal of second Infraction citing interpretation differences.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 23 states earlier decision-maker MC collaborated with CELL, noted misunderstandings, granted extensions, and found partial progress with disputes.

propositions.text: The Report emphasizes CELL's responsibility to correct Infractions under the registration program.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 24 states the earlier decision-maker's report highlights CELL's responsibility to correct Infractions.

propositions.text: The Report concludes suspension of CELL's registration is justified due to serious failures to implement corrective actions.
Senior management was informed of requirements but did not correct Infractions and requested removal of an Infraction due to differing interpretation from MC.
MC is the regulatory agency that developed and implemented the requirements.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 25 concludes earlier decision-maker MC justified suspension due to serious failures and management's refusal to correct Infractions.

propositions.text: Applicants argue suspension decision is unreasonable, based on erroneous data, arbitrary process, and lack of standardized procedure.
Applicants claim MC ignored their third corrective action plan, violating audi alteram partem rule.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 26 states applicants argue the suspension decision is unreasonable, based on errors and procedural flaws, and MC ignored their third corrective plan violating fairness.

propositions.text: Reformulated issues: Is the Decision unreasonable? Was the decision-making process by Ms. Allen procedurally fair?

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 27 states the court reformulated the issues as whether the Decision is unreasonable and if Ms. Allen's process was procedurally fair.

propositions.text: Respondent argues some applicant arguments are inadmissible as not in the Notice of Application, violating Federal Courts Rules 301e).

Respondent says applicants cannot raise: (i) suspension based on arbitrary process; (ii) suspension based on lack of standardized procedure; (iii) maintaining suspension ignoring third corrective plan violating audi alteram partem.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 28 states respondent argues some applicant arguments are inadmissible for not being in the Notice, listing three specific inadmissible arguments.

propositions.text: Respondent claims surprise and inability to respond to these arguments in affidavits due to timing of applicants' memorandum after affidavits.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 29 states respondent claims surprise and inability to respond to new arguments due to timing of applicants' memorandum after affidavits.

propositions.text: Applicants argue respondent had ample time to respond as arguments were in their memorandum.
Applicants intend to request oral amendment of Notice under Rule 75 to better define issues if court accepts respondent's argument.
Applicants argue procedural amendment should be allowed to clarify issues at hearing (Rule 75(2)(a)).

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 30 states applicants argue respondent had time to respond and intend to amend Notice orally under Rule 75 if needed to clarify issues.

propositions.text: Respondent says unclear Notice caused prejudice regarding evidence and oral amendment request is too late.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 31 states respondent says unclear Notice caused prejudice and applicants' oral amendment request is too late.

propositions.text: The decision under review is Ms. Allen's response to CELL's third appeal of the Suspension, not the suspension itself.
Court will examine applicants' arguments and reasonableness of the Decision in analysis.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 32 states the court clarifies the decision under review is Ms. Allen's response to the third appeal and will analyze arguments and reasonableness.

propositions.text: Applicants' grounds were not clearly specified in Notice but concerns about follow-up process, inspector training, feedback, MEN application, and suspension appropriateness are raised.
Applicants mention their third corrective action plan in the Notice.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 33 states the court finds applicants' grounds unclear but raising concerns about process, training, MEN, suspension, and mentioning third corrective plan.

propositions.text: Respondent knew applicants' issues by May 31, 2023 and addressed them in June 29, 2023 memorandum.
Respondent could have filed motion to strike or for leave to file additional affidavits; applicants could have filed motion to amend Notice since June 29, 2023.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 34 states the court finds respondent knew issues by May 31 and addressed them June 29; both parties could have filed procedural motions earlier.

propositions.text: Court will address applicants' substantive arguments to serve justice without delay, as neither party wants adjournment.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 35 states the court will address applicants' substantive arguments to serve justice without delay as no party wants adjournment.

propositions.text: Applicants orally request to file additional affidavit by Mr. Lamontagne with notes from meetings with MC representatives during hearing break.
Affidavit and attachment respond to court question about factual error allegation by inspector Vanasse regarding 'drain valve' of standard used by Ms. Lamontagne.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 36 states applicants orally request to file additional affidavit with notes responding to court question about factual error allegation by inspector Vanasse.

propositions.text: Respondent opposes late filing, describing evidence as interested and should have been in first affidavit.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 37 states respondent opposes late filing, calling evidence interested and should have been in first affidavit.

propositions.text: Rule 312 allows filing additional affidavits with court's discretion guided by principles from Forest Ethics and Bossé cases.
Preliminary requirements: evidence must be admissible and relevant; usually court reviews decision-maker's record.
Court considers if party had access to evidence when filing affidavits or could have with due diligence.
Court considers if evidence is useful, relevant, and probative to outcome.
Court considers if admitting evidence causes serious prejudice to other party.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 38 states court explains Rule 312 and principles for admitting additional affidavits including admissibility, relevance, diligence, usefulness, and prejudice.

propositions.text: Additional affidavit is inadmissible under Rule 312 because attachment was not before Ms. Allen and applicants had access when filing initial affidavit.
Probative value does not justify admission; respondent would suffer prejudice if evidence admitted at advanced stage.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 39 states court concludes additional affidavit inadmissible as attachment was not before Ms. Allen, applicants had access earlier, and admission causes prejudice.

propositions.text: Court rejects applicants' oral request to file Mr. Lamontagne's affidavit and attachment during hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 40 states court rejects applicants' oral request to file additional affidavit and attachment during hearing.

propositions.text: Les demandeurs allèguent que la formation de l’inspectrice Vanasse est déficiente et qu’elle a commis des erreurs factuelles
Ils contestent le processus aléatoire suivi par l’inspectrice et l’absence de procédures standardisées pour décider d’une suspension
Ils affirment que la décision de MC est déraisonnable car fondée sur des données erronées, des procédures aléatoires ou non-standardisées
Ils ne précisent pas quelle décision est mise en cause

paragraphs.summary: Les demandeurs allèguent une formation déficiente de l’inspectrice Vanasse, contestent le processus aléatoire et affirment que la décision de MC est déraisonnable, sans préciser la décision visée.

propositions.text: La décision sous contrôle est celle de Mme Allen de maintenir la Suspension, pas la décision de 2018 imposant la Suspension
La question ultime est si la décision aborde de façon transparente et intelligible les arguments du troisième appel de CELL
J’examinerai si les préoccupations factuelles et arguments des demandeurs minent le caractère raisonnable de la Décision

paragraphs.summary: La décision sous contrôle est celle de Mme Allen maintenant la Suspension; la Cour doit vérifier si elle répond raisonnablement aux arguments du troisième appel de CELL.

propositions.text: La norme de contrôle applicable est la norme de la décision raisonnable selon Vavilov

paragraphs.summary: La norme de contrôle applicable est la décision raisonnable selon Vavilov, établi par la Cour suprême du Canada.

propositions.text: La cour de révision doit vérifier si la décision est fondée sur une analyse cohérente, rationnelle et justifiée selon Vavilov
La décision doit posséder justification, transparence et intelligibilité selon Vavilov
La partie contestant la décision doit démontrer son caractère déraisonnable selon Vavilov

paragraphs.summary: Selon Vavilov, la cour doit vérifier si la décision est cohérente, justifiée, transparente et intelligible; le contestataire doit prouver son déraisonnable.

propositions.text: Les demandeurs n’ont pas identifié d’erreur révisable liée à la formation inadéquate de l’inspectrice Vanasse

paragraphs.summary: La Cour conclut que les demandeurs n’ont pas démontré d’erreur révisable sur la formation de l’inspectrice Vanasse.

propositions.text: L’inspectrice Vanasse n’a pas reçu la formation nécessaire pour l’examen de suivi du 23 février 2018
MC n’a fourni aucun détail sur la formation et la capacité de l’inspectrice à reconnaître la mise en œuvre correcte de l’étalon modèle 220L
La Suspension est basée sur des erreurs factuelles car MC a fondé ses décisions sur une personne non qualifiée

paragraphs.summary: Les demandeurs soutiennent que l’inspectrice Vanasse manquait de formation et que MC a fondé ses décisions sur une personne non qualifiée.

propositions.text: Le Rapport fait erronément référence à une valve d’égouttement, alors que l’étalon modèle 220L n’en a pas
Il y a donc des erreurs dans le rapport de l’inspectrice sur les résultats de l’examen de suivi

paragraphs.summary: Les demandeurs affirment que le rapport mentionne à tort une valve d’égouttement, ce qui entraîne des erreurs dans le rapport de l’inspectrice.

propositions.text: La formation de l'inspectrice Vanasse a été discutée et critiquée lors des deux premiers appels de la Suspension
M. Lamontagne estime que l’inspectrice ne s’était pas adéquatement préparée pour l’examen de suivi
La formation de l’inspectrice n’a pas été soulevée à nouveau dans le troisième appel, mais a été discutée lors des contre-interrogatoires

paragraphs.summary: La formation de l’inspectrice Vanasse a été critiquée lors des deux premiers appels, pas soulevée dans le troisième, mais discutée en contre-interrogatoires.

propositions.text: L’argument sur la valve d’égouttement apparaît pour la première fois dans l’Avis de demande des demandeurs
L’étalon modèle 220L n’a pas de valve d’égouttement mais une valve de drainage
Ce point est un argument principal pour démontrer que l’inspectrice n’avait pas reçu une formation adéquate

paragraphs.summary: L’argument sur l’absence de valve d’égouttement est nouveau et principal pour démontrer un manque de formation de l’inspectrice.

propositions.text: Les demandeurs n’ont pas contesté l’existence d’une valve d’égouttement ou de vidange/drainage dans leurs appels ni dans leur mémoire
M. Lamontagne a indiqué que l’inspectrice ne connaissait pas son chariot-étalon, sans mentionner l’absence de valve d’égouttement

paragraphs.summary: Les demandeurs n’ont jamais contesté l’existence d’une valve d’égouttement ou vidange, ni soulevé ce point dans leur mémoire.

propositions.text: Les mots « valve d’égouttement » n’apparaissent pas dans les notes de l’inspectrice Vanasse
L’inspectrice a évalué la MEN 22 et conclu que l’égouttement n’avait pas été exécuté adéquatement
L’inspectrice a noté que la valve reste ouverte plusieurs fois et que la durée de vidange a été mentionnée
L’avocat des demandeurs a dit qu’une valve d’égouttement et une valve de vidange ne sont pas synonymes
Seuls MC et CELL ont mentionné une valve d’égouttement, pas l’inspectrice Vanasse

paragraphs.summary: Les notes de l’inspectrice ne mentionnent pas de valve d’égouttement, seulement des observations sur la valve et la vidange; seuls MC et CELL ont utilisé ce terme.

propositions.text: MC a utilisé la phrase « valve d’égouttement » dans ses observations sur le plan d’action correctif
Les parties semblent avoir adopté cette expression

paragraphs.summary: MC a utilisé l’expression « valve d’égouttement » dans ses observations, que les parties ont adoptée.

propositions.text: CELL n’a pas contesté l’existence d’une valve d’égouttement dans la troisième version de son plan
CELL a remis en question les exigences et procédures de MC concernant l’étalon et le temps d’égouttement
Un extrait du deuxième appel de CELL affirme que la valve ouverte rendrait impossible la prise de lecture du liquide

paragraphs.summary: CELL n’a pas contesté la valve d’égouttement mais a remis en question les exigences de MC; elle affirme que valve ouverte empêcherait la lecture du liquide.

propositions.text: J’ai demandé si la question de la valve d’égouttement avait été soulevée lors du troisième appel
L’avocat des demandeurs a répondu que l’étalon modèle 220L n’avait pas de valve d’égouttement
J’ai expliqué que la Cour ne peut déterminer si un étalon porte une valve d’égouttement ou de vidange
Le rôle de la Cour est de déterminer si la question a été soulevée devant la décideuse et si elle a été abordée raisonnablement
L’avocat a dit que la formation de l’inspectrice Vanasse avait été posée lors du troisième appel
Les demandeurs avaient demandé une révision complète du dossier et Mme Allen avait pu constater que l’étalon n’avait pas de valve d’égouttement

paragraphs.summary: La Cour a demandé si la valve d’égouttement avait été soulevée; l’avocat a dit que oui, via la formation, et que Mme Allen avait pu constater l’absence de valve.

propositions.text: Les demandeurs devaient soulever leurs arguments lors du troisième appel, pas pour la première fois devant la Cour
Il ne suffit pas de demander une révision complète et soulever ensuite de nouveaux arguments techniques devant la Cour
Je n’aborderai pas l’argument sur la valve d’égouttement car il n’a pas été soulevé dans le troisième appel

paragraphs.summary: La Cour rejette l’argument sur la valve d’égouttement car il n’a pas été soulevé lors du troisième appel, ce qui était requis.

propositions.text: Les demandeurs soulignent que l’inspectrice n’a pas été formée sur l’étalon modèle 220L car M. Lamontagne est seul à pouvoir fournir cette formation
Par conséquent, elle n’avait pas la formation nécessaire pour les inspections du 23 février 2018
MC répond que tous ses inspecteurs reçoivent les formations nécessaires
Les demandeurs déclarent que MC n’a produit aucune preuve de la formation de l’inspectrice Vanasse

paragraphs.summary: Les demandeurs affirment que l’inspectrice n’a pas reçu la formation nécessaire; MC dit que tous ses inspecteurs sont formés; demandeurs contestent preuve.

propositions.text: Les demandeurs se basent sur des extraits des contre-interrogatoires de M. Parent et M. Bourdon
Les demandeurs ne tiennent pas compte des réponses complètes des témoins
Les demandeurs allèguent que M. Parent ne pouvait pas indiquer si l’inspectrice avait reçu une formation sur l’étalon 220L
MC souligne que M. Parent dit que la formation sur l’étalon de M. Lamontagne n’existe pas mais n’est pas nécessaire
M. Parent explique que l’inspectrice n’a pas besoin de connaître tous les étalons car c’est la technicienne qui opère l’étalon
Le rôle de l’inspectrice est de s’assurer que l’opération respecte les méthodes d’essais normalisées
La MEN est identique pour tous les étalons, toujours un étalon calibré avec une façon d’égoutter

paragraphs.summary: Les demandeurs citent des extraits de témoins, mais MC explique que la formation spécifique n’est pas nécessaire car l’inspectrice vérifie la conformité aux méthodes normalisées.

propositions.text: M. Bourdon confirme qu’aucune formation n’était requise pour l’examen de suivi
L’inspectrice avait pris connaissance des particularités de l’étalon, suffisant pour l’examen
L’inspectrice ne manipulait pas l’étalon, ce sont les techniciens qui l’utilisent

paragraphs.summary: M. Bourdon confirme qu’aucune formation n’était requise, l’inspectrice connaissait l’étalon et ne l’utilisait pas, ce sont les techniciens qui l’utilisent.

propositions.text: Les demandeurs soutiennent que l’examen de suivi a été fait avec des distributrices défectueuses
Un autre FSA a réparé les distributrices
Ils demandent pourquoi MC a suspendu CELL et non le FSA responsable des infractions sur les distributeurs

paragraphs.summary: Les demandeurs affirment que l’examen a utilisé des distributrices défectueuses et demandent pourquoi MC a suspendu CELL et non le FSA responsable.

propositions.text: Mme Allen a répondu que la surveillance de MC vise la conformité du travail des techniciens, pas seulement des appareils
MC n’a pas identifié le FSA comme responsable des non-conformités lors de l’examen de suivi
CELL a été suspendu pour non-respect des exigences du programme d’enregistrement, pas pour les non-conformités des distributeurs

paragraphs.summary: Mme Allen a expliqué que MC surveille la conformité des techniciens, a suspendu CELL pour non-respect du programme, pas pour non-conformités des distributeurs.

propositions.text: Mme Allen's response is intelligible and transparent.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mme Allen's response intelligible and transparent.

propositions.text: Applicants did not demonstrate the Decision was based on erroneous data from the 2018 follow-up review.
MC addressed applicants' questions about inspector Vanasse's training.
Mr. Parent and Mr. Bourdon answered clearly and convincingly in cross-examinations.
Mme Allen was not questioned on alleged error about valve references in inspector's notes.
Applicants disagree with decision-maker and MC's conclusions but court will not reweigh evidence.
Court will not determine if inspector Vanasse had necessary training or difference between valve types.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes applicants failed to show the Decision was based on erroneous data; MC and witnesses addressed training questions; court will not reweigh evidence or decide on training or valve differences.

propositions.text: Decision to suspend CELL was unreasonable due to random processes and procedures in follow-up review.
MC inspectors do not use standardized forms or checklists, making consistent reviews impossible.
Mr. Bourdon confirmed no standard method and communication is random.
Mr. Bourdon said MC did not provide training or help to CELL.
Applicants conclude MC's decision is unreasonable based on random procedures and processes.
Applicants do not specify which decision they refer to.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue suspension decision was unreasonable due to random procedures, lack of standardized forms, no training, but do not specify which decision.

propositions.text: Applicants selectively quoted cross-examinations and omitted other parts.
Applicants claim Mr. Bourdon said no training or help was given by MC.
Mr. Bourdon stated he personally tried to help Mr. Lamontagne with infractions.
Mr. Bourdon's affidavit contradicts applicants' claim about lack of help.
Applicants say Mr. Bourdon described method as non-standard and random regarding use of standardized form.
Mr. Bourdon confirmed reports could be recorded in Word, Excel, or other programs.
Mr. Parent explained inspectors must follow MC's process and complete all steps in order despite no standardized form.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds applicants selectively quoted Mr. Bourdon, who stated he helped Lamontagne; Mr. Parent explained inspectors follow MC's process despite no standard form.

propositions.text: Mr. Parent confirmed CELL and Mr. Lamontagne received help during cross-examination.
Timeline in applicants' memorandum and Decision Annex 2 shows help MC provided to applicants.
Applicants wrote they requested guidance from Mr. Bourdon on March 5, 2018, and received responses.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Parent confirmed help was given; timeline and applicants' own memorandum show MC provided assistance.

propositions.text: Applicants did not explain which aspects of follow-up review were random beyond lack of standardized form and alleged lack of help.
Applicants failed to show how alleged deficiencies made the Decision unreasonable.
Applicants did not raise a reviewable error in the Decision convincingly.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds applicants did not explain randomness aspects or show how deficiencies made Decision unreasonable; no reviewable error raised.

propositions.text: MC did not follow a standardized procedure to impose Suspension.
Mr. Parent said no exact process leads to suspension and partial/full suspensions are used randomly.
Applicants say infractions were minor and MC could have taken other reasonable measures.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege MC used no standardized procedure for Suspension; Mr. Parent said suspensions are used randomly; infractions were minor.

propositions.text: Mr. Parent explained serious infractions impacting commerce can lead directly to suspension.
Mr. Parent distinguished minor and major infractions.
MC considers several factors before imposing partial or full suspension.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Parent explained serious infractions can lead to suspension and MC considers multiple factors before suspending.

propositions.text: Applicants did not convince court Suspension resulted from non-standard and unreasonable procedure.
Paragraph 16.1(3) of the Act and articles 1.8.4 and 1.11 of the Terms provide for suspension in case of serious breaches.
Application of suspension depends on severity, impact on fairness and accuracy, whether accidental or intentional, and frequency.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes applicants failed to prove Suspension was from non-standard procedure; law provides suspension for serious breaches based on severity and other factors.

propositions.text: Mme Allen detailed infractions and explained CELL was suspended because infractions were unresolved despite exchanges.
Suspension clearly indicates relevant MEN and MC's reasons for the two infractions.
Court must focus on rendered Decision and not reweigh evidence or draw own conclusion (Lalonde 2023 CF 41 para 29).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Mme Allen detailed infractions and reasons for suspension; court must focus on Decision and not reweigh evidence.

propositions.text: Applicants' arguments largely contest MC's September 8, 2018 suspension decision and indirectly the Decision.
Court examined each argument under third appeal, six questions by Mr. Lamontagne, Mme Allen's responses, evidence, transcripts, written and oral arguments, Decision and Report.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes applicants contest MC's suspension decision and examined all arguments, questions, evidence, and Decision under third appeal.

propositions.text: Mme Allen conducted rigorous analysis before concluding Suspension was justified and would be maintained.
Mme Allen clearly explained scope of appeal analysis and reasons in Decision and Report.
Analysis of evidence underlying conclusions is coherent, rational, and justified under legal and factual constraints (Vavilov para 85).
Decision meets Supreme Court of Canada standards for administrative decisions to be reasonable, transparent, intelligible, and justified (Vavilov paras 15, 99).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mme Allen's analysis was rigorous, clear, and met Supreme Court standards for reasonable administrative decisions.

propositions.text: Applicants argue Mme Allen's Decision to maintain Suspension without considering third corrective action plan violates audi alteram partem rule.
Applicants say Decision prevents CELL from operating and Mr. Lamontagne from earning a living, highlighting Decision's importance.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue Mme Allen's Decision violated procedural fairness by ignoring third corrective plan, impacting CELL's business and Mr. Lamontagne's livelihood.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness concerns the decision-making process, not the decision's merits.
Procedural fairness includes right to be heard and respond to evidence, and right to fair, impartial hearing before independent tribunal (Therrien 2001 CSC 35 para 82).

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness concerns process, including right to be heard and impartial hearing, not decision merits.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal says procedural fairness issues are not decided by a particular standard of review.
Reviewing court must determine if decision-making procedure was fair considering all circumstances (CCP para 54).
Analysis includes five contextual factors from Supreme Court in Baker (1999) and Vavilov para 77.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains procedural fairness is assessed on fairness of procedure in context, per Federal Court of Appeal and Supreme Court precedents.

propositions.text: Applicants' argument that MC and Mme Allen ignored third corrective action plan is without merit.
Mme Allen stated the Report was attached to inform CELL of points assessed by MC in third appeal.
Report states three versions of corrective plans submitted by CELL did not meet regulatory or program requirements.
MC provided explanations and advice to assist Mr. Lamontagne to correct infractions for each plan version.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds applicants' claim that MC and Mme Allen ignored third corrective plan is without merit; Report shows plans were assessed and advice given.

propositions.text: Mme Allen confirmed in Report she considered CELL's last attempt to resolve infractions: third corrective plan received in two parts in August 2018.
Progress was made on first infraction but CELL sought removal of second due to interpretation differences with MC.
Evidence including Mr. Parent's affidavit and cross-examination shows MC evaluated CELL's third plan.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mme Allen considered CELL's third corrective plan; progress noted on first infraction; evidence shows MC evaluated the plan.

propositions.text: MC considered CELL's third plan.
Timeline shows interactive process with many opportunities for CELL to present arguments, evidence, and understand MC's reasoning.
Appeal regime has three levels; at third appeal, applicants could ask written questions and Mme Allen responded.
Multiple meetings and communications occurred between CELL and MC representatives.
Despite no feedback after third corrective plan submission, process was fair and participatory.
CELL and Mr. Lamontagne knew evidence to refute and had full fair opportunity to respond (CCP para 56).
MC was not required to provide further feedback or allow another corrective plan revision opportunity.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds MC considered third plan; process was interactive, fair, and participatory; applicants had full opportunity to respond; no further feedback required.

propositions.text: Applicants suggested MC decided early and did not consider CELL's evidence, raising bias issue.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege MC decided early and ignored CELL's evidence, raising bias concerns.

propositions.text: Applicants raised bias allegation late.
Applicants referenced Baker para 45 and importance of administrative decision-maker impartiality without explanation amid data error allegations.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds applicants raised bias allegation late, referencing Baker para 45 and impartiality without explanation amid data error claims.

propositions.text: The test for reasonable apprehension of bias is well established and requires a high threshold.
The test asks what a well-informed, reasonable person would conclude after a realistic and practical study of the issue.
Baker states the decision-maker might not render a fair decision consciously or unconsciously.
Allegations of bias cannot rest solely on impressions or suspicions of the applicant.
Allegations of bias are serious and must be supported by concrete evidence.
Arthur requires serious allegations of bias to be supported by evidence.
The burden of proof lies on the party alleging reasonable apprehension of bias.
Zhou confirms the burden of proof on the alleging party for bias claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the high threshold and test for reasonable apprehension of bias, requiring concrete evidence and burden on the alleging party, citing Baker, Arthur, and Zhou.

propositions.text: Applicants allege bias because Mr. Parent was always present and had influence with Ms. Allen.
Allegations of bias must be demonstrated with concrete evidence, not lightly raised.
Alvarez confirms that bias allegations require concrete proof.
Applicants produced no evidence to support their bias allegation here.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege bias due to Mr. Parent's presence and influence, but the court finds no concrete evidence was produced, citing Alvarez.

propositions.text: The court rejects the applicants' allegation of bias.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the applicants' allegation of bias.

propositions.text: The applicants' application for judicial review is dismissed for all reasons stated.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the applicants' judicial review application for all reasons given.

propositions.text: With parties' consent and Rule 303(1), the style of cause is amended to correctly name the respondent as the Attorney General of Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court amends the style of cause to correctly name the Attorney General of Canada as respondent, with parties' consent and Rule 303(1).

propositions.text: At hearing conclusion, parties agreed to consult and advise the court if they agreed on costs amount.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes parties agreed to consult and advise on costs amount after hearing.

propositions.text: Parties informed the court by letter dated December 12, 2023, they agreed the winning party would receive $4,000 in costs from the losing party.

paragraphs.summary: Parties informed the court they agreed the winning party would receive $4,000 costs from the losing party.

propositions.text: The court sees no reason to depart from the general rule that costs follow the result.
Given all circumstances, the court agrees the agreed $4,000 costs amount is reasonable and justified.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no reason to depart from costs following the result and agrees $4,000 costs amount is reasonable and justified.

propositions.text: The court awards the respondent $4,000 in costs.
The judicial review application is dismissed; style of cause amended to name Attorney General of Canada as respondent; costs awarded to respondent.

paragraphs.summary: The court awards respondent $4,000 costs, dismisses judicial review, and amends style of cause to name Attorney General of Canada as respondent.
